newsitem.title: INDIA: Renowned criminal on verge of going free in India.
newsitem.headline: Renowned criminal on verge of going free in India.

text.p: An Indian judge on Friday ordered notorious criminal Charles Sobhraj freed from prison on bail, but his release after nearly two decades behind bars was held up by last-minute formalities, authorities said.

About 100 reporters waited for several hours outside maximum-security Tihar jail, Asia's biggest prison, after Judge Y.S. Jonwal ordered the 58-year-old Sobhraj released on a personal bond and surety of 50,000 rupees ($1,400).
Sobhraj's lawyer, Rajan Bakshi, said his client had expected to walk out of prison on Friday afternoon.
But authorities said his release had been delayed. "Some formalities are pending so we are not releasing him today," police superintendent Yashpal Garg told reporters.
"I don't know the reason for detainment," Bakshi said. "If they are not going to release him before Monday, I'll file a case of illegal confinement."
Prison and court authorities could not be reached for comment.
Sobhraj, a French citizen born to an Indian father and a Vietnamese mother, was in detention in connection with a 1986 jailbreak case.
Sobhraj was first arrested in India for holding up a hotel jewellery shop in 1971. The gaunt, good-looking 26-year-old jumped bail before his trial could be held.

The suave, multilingual criminal was first convicted in 1978 of robbing and murdering a French tourist by slipping drugs into his chicken curry before stealing his travellers' cheques. He was acquitted 20 months later.
Since then, Sobhraj has been in and out of Indian jails on charges of murder, drug-peddling and robbery, often chained in iron fetters and in solitary confinement.
He was convicted in 1978 of drugging and robbing a group of French tourists near India's fabled Taj Mahal monument, for which he served a five-year prison term.
A judge sentenced him to life imprisonment in 1982 for poisoning an Israeli tourist to death. He was acquitted in 1983.
Two books and a film have been made about Sobhraj.
He shot to fame in 1986 when he fled from New Delhi's Tihar Jail, where he was in detention pending an extradition request from Thailand to face charges of murder and attempted murder.
In November 1995 Thai police said he could not be extradited to stand trial in that country because a 20-year statute of limitations had expired.

Kiran Bedi, a crusading policewoman who turned the grimy Tihar jail inside out in two years as inspector-general of prisons by teaching inmates to read and introducing meditation to hardened criminals, irked her superiors by allowing Sobhraj to have a Walkman tape recorder, a TV and a typewriter.
Sobhraj's lawyer said the only case now pending against his client was the 1986 jail escape. If released on bail, he would not be allowed to leave India.
